artists.biography:
Orville Peck is a country musician based in Canada. He wears a fringed mask and has never shown his face publicly. He released his debut album Pony in 2019, followed by the EP Show Pony the next year.
Peck was born in Johannesburg, South Africa and lived there until he was 15. As a child, Peck did not receive any formal music training, he taught himself music by playing on an acoustic guitar and an old Casio keyboard. He is the son of a sound engineer, and he did voice-over work for cartoons and other media as a child. Growing up, he trained in ballet for 12 years, and performed in musical theatre. By the time he was in his early 20s, Peck had been on national tours of musicals.

In his mid-20s, he moved to London to study acting at the London Academy of Music and Dramatic Art, and later starred in a play on the West End.

apple_music.editorial_notes: Orville Peck might be known for hiding his face behind playful bedazzled masks, but the acclaimed singer-songwriter truly lays himself bare on this fourth studio album and follow-up to 2024’s Stampede. Produced by Jay Joyce (Eric Church, Molly Tuttle), Mule is a vulnerable account of Peck’s battle with addiction and journey to sobriety, and unsurprisingly features his rawest songwriting yet. Structured as a concept album telling a chronological story, Mule opens with “Prologue (Eulogy of a Man Turned Mule)”, a gorgeous overture performed by Emmylou Harris, Allison Russell and Noah Cyrus, who harmonise like an angel choir. It leads right into “Big Ol’ House”, a potent and dramatic rocker that also functions as a laundry list of Peck’s regrets: “Drink all night and start a fight/Take someone home that I don’t know.” “Rehab Blues” painstakingly details the more quotidian horrors of getting clean, like forfeiting privacy and reliving past trauma, with Peck’s vocal theatrics reinforcing the absurdity of existence rather than lightening the mood. The back half of the LP makes room for redemption, like on standout “The Breeze, the Grass, the Mourning Dove and Me,” a gently rolling ballad on which Peck invites a lover to trust him again. Peck closes with “Mule”, on which he takes stock of how far he’s come, expresses fear for the future and finally makes peace—if shakily—with his difficult past. “You can look back with regret,” he sings, “but you’re bound to hurt your neck.”

perplexity.description:
Orville Peck’s Mule is a stark, deeply personal fourth studio album that turns the mask of his persona toward a more exposed, autobiographical story. Built around classic country, Americana, bluegrass, and folk-leaning textures, the record traces a difficult year marked by addiction, treatment, sobriety, heartbreak, and recovery, with songs arranged as a chronological narrative rather than a loose collection of singles.

Released by Warner Records in 2026, Mule has been described as Peck’s most candid work to date, balancing wrenching confession with the widescreen emotional sweep that has defined his best material. Its significance lies in the way it pushes his outlaw-country aesthetic into more intimate, vulnerable territory, reinforcing his reputation as one of modern country’s most distinctive and emotionally direct voices.
